blocks.text: Imagine writing a program that sorts a list. How can you be sure it always works correctly, for every possible input?

blocks.markdown: In programming, it's crucial to ensure that code behaves as expected. Rather than relying solely on testing, we can use logical reasoning to prove a program's correctness. This is where preconditions and postconditions come into play, forming the basis of Hoare logic.

blocks.title: Hoare Triple
blocks.text: A Hoare triple is a formalism used to reason about the correctness of computer programs. It is written as \( \{P\} \ C \ \{Q\} \), where \(P\) is the precondition, \(C\) is the command or program, and \(Q\) is the postcondition.

blocks.markdown: The precondition \(P\) specifies what must be true before the execution of the program \(C\). The postcondition \(Q\) specifies what must be true after the execution of \(C\), assuming \(P\) was true initially.

blocks.caption: Example of a Hoare triple where the precondition and postcondition are simple inequalities.

blocks.markdown: In this example, the precondition \(x > 0\) ensures that the variable \(x\) is positive before the command \(x := x + 1\) is executed. The postcondition \(x > 1\) guarantees that \(x\) will be greater than 1 after the execution.

blocks.title: Simple Assignment
blocks.prompt: Consider the Hoare triple \( \{x = 2\} \ x := x + 3 \ \{x = 5\} \). Prove its correctness.
blocks.answer: The Hoare triple is correct because the postcondition is satisfied after executing the command.

blocks.markdown: Hoare logic distinguishes between partial and total correctness. Partial correctness ensures that if a program terminates, the postcondition will be true. Total correctness includes partial correctness and also guarantees that the program will terminate.

blocks.title: Partial vs Total Correctness
blocks.text: Partial correctness: \( \{P\} \ C \ \{Q\} \) holds if whenever \(P\) is true and \(C\) terminates, \(Q\) is true. Total correctness: \( \{P\} \ C \ \{Q\} \) holds if \(C\) always terminates and \(Q\) is true whenever \(P\) is true.

blocks.title: Loop Example
blocks.prompt: Consider the loop: \( \{x > 0\} \ \text{while} \ (x > 0) \ \{x := x - 1\} \ \{x = 0\} \). Discuss its correctness.

steps.text: The precondition \(x > 0\) ensures the loop starts with a positive \(x\).
The postcondition \(x = 0\) is reached when the loop terminates.
The loop will terminate as \(x\) decreases by 1 each iteration.

blocks.answer: The Hoare triple is totally correct because the loop terminates and the postcondition is satisfied.

blocks.title: Infinite Loops
blocks.text: Be cautious of infinite loops. They can satisfy partial correctness but fail total correctness due to non-termination.

points: Hoare triples provide a formal way to reason about program correctness.
Partial correctness ensures the postcondition holds if the program terminates.
Total correctness includes termination in addition to partial correctness.
